target: Eu estou com calor.
english: I'm hot.
old: Portuguese says 'I am with hunger' (`estou com fome`) – different from Spanish (`tengo`) and French (`j'ai faim`). Same structure for `estou com sede` (thirsty), `estou com pressa` (in a hurry).
focus: Body states use estar com + noun; anchor on this card's 'estou com calor', keep the Spanish tengo / French j'ai contrast, strip backticks

target: Eu tenho muito sono.
english: I'm very sleepy.
old: 'Ter sono' means 'to be sleepy.' Portuguese uses 'ter' (to have) for many physical and emotional states: ter fome, ter sede, ter sono, ter pressa.
focus: 'tenho muito sono' is literally 'I have much sleep'; keep the ter-state insight but drop the ter fome/sede list, which clashes with the deck's estar-com guidance

target: Ela cozinha muito bem.
english: She cooks very well.
old: 'Cozinhar' follows regular -ar patterns. 'Cozinha' means both 'cooks' (verb) and 'kitchen' (noun).
focus: cozinha = both 'she cooks' and 'kitchen'; drop the regular -ar-pattern clause

target: Eles têm três filhos.
english: They have three children.
old: 'Têm' (with circumflex) is the eles/elas form of 'ter.' The accent distinguishes it from 'tem' (ele/ela form). This is an important spelling distinction.
focus: têm (eles/elas) vs tem (ele/ela) circumflex; cut the 'this is an important spelling distinction' filler clause

target: Eu sei que ele está ocupado.
english: I know he's busy.
old: `estar` for how you are right now – mood, health, location, temporary state. Wrong: `sou cansado` (I'm a tired *person*). Right: `estou cansado` (I'm tired *today*).
focus: estar for right-now states; re-anchor the example on this card's 'está ocupado' (busy now, not a busy person) and strip backticks

target: Ele faz exercício todo dia de manhã.
english: He exercises every morning.
old: 'Fazer' is irregular: eu faço, ele faz. 'Todo dia' = every day – 'todo' + singular = every.
focus: 'todo dia': todo + singular = every; drop the fazer conjugation list

target: Eu estou com saudade dos meus amigos.
english: I miss my friends.
old: Watch: fome, sede, sono, frio, calor, medo, pressa, raiva, saudade – all take `estar com` in BR. Direct translation 'I am hungry' (`sou faminto`) sounds bizarre.
focus: estar com saudade = missing someone; keep the estar-com family point but anchor on saudade, trim the nine-noun list, strip backticks

target: Você gosta de cozinhar?
english: Do you like to cook?
old: 'Gostar de' always requires the preposition 'de' – never drop it. You'll learn more in node-06.
focus: gostar always needs de before its object (English 'like' takes none); remove the 'node-06' meta reference

target: Vocês comem fora com frequência?
english: Do you eat out often?
old: Portuguese has two `you`s: `tu` (informal, PT/southern BR) and `você` (universal in BR). Different verb forms: `tu falas` vs `você fala`.
focus: sole surviving tu/você telling: anchor on 'vocês' as the universal you-plural in Brazil, tu regional; strip backticks

target: Ele está no escritório agora.
english: He's at the office now.
old: 'Estar' for temporary location: 'ele está no escritório.' 'No' = em + o. Location uses estar, not ser.
focus: one rule only: estar (not ser) for where someone is right now, anchored on 'está no escritório'; drop the no=em+o aside

target: Eu posso trazer um amigo?
english: Can I bring a friend?
old: 'Trazer' means to bring and is irregular: trago, traz, trazemos, trazem. Don't confuse with 'levar' (to take away from here).
focus: trazer (bring here) vs levar (take away), anchored on 'posso trazer'; drop the conjugation list

target: Eu quero um café, por favor.
english: I want a coffee, please.
old: 'Querer' is irregular: quero, quer, queremos, querem. It's less blunt in Portuguese than 'I want' in English – perfectly polite with 'por favor.'
focus: 'quero um café, por favor' is perfectly polite, none of English 'I want' bluntness; drop the conjugation list

target: Ela está trabalhando de casa hoje.
english: She's working from home today.
old: `estar + gerúndio` = English '-ing right now': `estou comendo` = 'I'm eating'. Brazilians use this way more than Spanish/Italian use their gerundios.
focus: estar + -ndo = English -ing in progress, anchored on 'está trabalhando'; strip backticks

target: Você trabalha de segunda a sexta?
english: Do you work Monday through Friday?
old: Yes/no questions in Portuguese often have the same word order as statements – intonation does the work.
focus: Anchor in this card: 'Você trabalha...?' keeps plain statement order – no 'do', rising intonation alone makes it a question.

target: Nós voltamos para casa às seis.
english: We go back home at six.
old: 'Em casa' = at home (no article). 'Na casa dele' = at his house (article needed with possessive).
focus: Card says 'para casa', not 'em casa' – anchor on 'para casa': casa meaning 'home' takes no article; with an article it's someone's house.

target: Nós gostamos de caminhar à noite.
english: We like to walk at night.
old: Portuguese `gostar` always takes `de`: `gosto de pizza`, `gosto de você`. Drop the `de` and the sentence breaks. English `like` has no preposition; Portuguese needs one.
focus: Strip backticks and tighten: gostar always takes de – quote 'gostamos de caminhar' from this card as the worked example.

target: Eu sei onde fica o restaurante.
english: I know where the restaurant is.
old: 'Saber' means to know facts or how to do something. 'Sei' is the irregular eu form. 'Ficar' meaning 'to be located' is very Brazilian.
focus: One rule only: 'fica' = 'is located' – ficar for where things sit is very Brazilian; drop the saber conjugation notes.

target: Eu vou fazer compras no shopping.
english: I'm going shopping at the mall.
old: 'Ir + infinitive' forms the immediate future in Brazilian Portuguese. It's used much more often than the simple future tense in everyday speech.
focus: Good insight, not anchored: quote 'vou fazer' from this card as the worked example of ir + infinitive as the everyday future.

target: Vocês podem vir para o jantar?
english: Can you come over for dinner?
old: 'Vir' means to come and is irregular: venho, vem, vimos, vêm. Don't confuse 'vir' (to come) with 'ver' (to see).
focus: Keep only the vir vs ver landmine, anchored on 'vir' in this card; drop the conjugation list.

target: O hotel é perto da praia.
english: The hotel is near the beach.
old: 'Ser' is used for permanent location of buildings and landmarks – use 'estar' for people and movable things.
focus: Quote 'é perto da praia'; ser for the fixed location of buildings and landmarks – the surprise is that location is not automatically estar.

target: Onde tem um bom restaurante japonês?
english: Where can I find a good Japanese restaurant?
old: Brazilians use `tem` for 'there is/are' instead of `há`: `tem uma farmácia aqui` = 'there's a pharmacy here'. Same `ter` (to have) doing double duty.
focus: Strip backticks; anchor on 'Onde tem' – Brazilians use tem for 'there is/are' where textbooks say há.

target: Ele é o mais velho dos irmãos.
english: He's the oldest of the siblings.
old: Prepositions and articles fuse: de + o → do, de + a → da, em + o → no, em + a → na. Gender info still shows: na casa is feminine.
focus: One rule, anchored: 'dos' = de + os from this card; cut the full fusion table and the off-card 'na casa' example.

target: Eu sou casado e tenho dois filhos.
english: I'm married and have two children.
old: Marital status uses 'ser' in Portuguese because it's seen as a defining characteristic, not a temporary state.
focus: Quote 'sou casado'; marital status takes ser in Portuguese – keep it to that one fact.

target: Eu estou com fome, vamos comer alguma coisa?
english: I'm hungry, shall we eat something?
old: 'Estar' expresses temporary states, conditions, and locations – things that could be different tomorrow.
focus: The real hook is in the card: 'estou com fome' is literally 'I'm with hunger' – estar com + noun for body states; drop the generic estar rule.

target: Ela mora num apartamento perto do centro.
english: She lives in an apartment near downtown.
old: Regular -ar verbs: morar → eu moro, ela mora. 'Num' is the contraction of 'em + um' (in a).
focus: Drop the morar conjugation; keep only num = em + um, quoting 'num apartamento' from this card.

target: Ela está ocupada agora, pode ligar depois.
english: She's busy now, you can call later.
old: 'Estar' is used for temporary states and emotions – how someone feels right now, not permanently.
focus: Estar for right-now states of people is worth keeping – anchor it by quoting 'está ocupada agora' instead of the generic statement.

target: Nós aproveitamos o feriado para descansar.
english: We take advantage of the holiday to rest.
old: 'Aproveitar' means 'to take advantage of' or 'to make the most of.' Brazilians use it constantly: 'aproveita!' means 'enjoy!'
focus: Cut the double gloss of the english field; the earner is the everyday imperative 'aproveita!' = enjoy!, anchored to 'aproveitamos o feriado'.

target: Vocês usam o metrô para ir ao trabalho?
english: Do you take the subway to get to work?
old: Regular -ar verbs: usar → vocês usam. Question formed purely by intonation, no word order change.
focus: Drop the usar conjugation; keep the real insight: yes/no questions are just statement word order + rising intonation, quoting 'Vocês usam o metrô?'.

target: Ele vai começar um curso novo mês que vem.
english: He's going to start a new course next month.
old: 'Ir' + infinitive is the everyday way to express future plans in Brazilian Portuguese – much more common than the simple future.
focus: Insight is right (ir + infinitive beats simple future in speech) but the tip never quotes this card – anchor with 'vai começar'.

target: Eu estou aprendendo português.
english: I'm learning Portuguese.
old: 'Estar' + gerund (-ando/-endo/-indo) forms the present continuous. Brazilians use this tense much more than the simple present for ongoing actions.
focus: Keep the estar + -ndo continuous point but quote 'estou aprendendo' from this card; the current tip only cites the abstract endings.

target: A água do mar é salgada.
english: Seawater is salty.
old: Inherent, defining characteristics use 'ser.' Seawater is always salty – it's in its nature.
focus: Ser for inherent traits is right, but the tip never quotes the card ('ser' can't match 'é') – anchor with 'a água do mar é salgada'.

target: Onde fica o banheiro?
english: Where is the bathroom?
old: 'Onde' means 'where.' In Brazil, 'ficar' is more natural than 'ser' or 'estar' when asking for locations.
focus: Cut ''onde' means where'; the earner is that Brazilians use ficar for locations – anchor with 'Onde fica o banheiro?'.

target: Eu dou aulas de português.
english: I give Portuguese lessons.
old: 'Dar' is irregular: dou, dá, damos, dão. 'Dar aulas' means to teach/give classes – a very common expression.
focus: Drop the dou/da/damos/dao listing; keep 'dar aulas' = to teach, quoting 'dou aulas' from this card.

target: Nós estamos planejando uma viagem.
english: We're planning a trip.
old: `estar + gerúndio` = English '-ing right now': `estou comendo` = 'I'm eating'. Brazilians use this way more than Spanish/Italian use their gerundios.
focus: Strip backticks and anchor in this card: 'estamos planejando' = estar + gerund is English '-ing right now', and Brazilians use it constantly.

target: Qual é o seu número de telefone?
english: What's your phone number?
old: 'Qual é' = what is (choosing/identifying). 'Número de telefone' = phone number.
focus: The real trap: Portuguese asks 'Qual é' (which is), not 'o que', for phone numbers and names – cut the 'número de telefone' vocab gloss.

target: Onde tem uma farmácia por perto?
english: Where is there a pharmacy nearby?
old: `Há` exists in PT but sounds formal/written. `Tem` is what you'll hear in speech. Same word as the verb 'to have' – context tells you which.
focus: Strip backticks, quote 'tem uma farmácia' from this card: spoken Brazilian uses tem for 'there is'; há sounds formal/written.

target: Nós vamos ao cinema hoje à noite.
english: We're going to the movies tonight.
old: 'Ir' is highly irregular: eu vou, nós vamos, vocês vão. 'Ir a' = to go to (with article: 'ao cinema').
focus: Keep only the contraction: 'ao cinema' = a + o fused; cut the vou/vamos/vão irregular-forms listing (the conjugation table covers it).

target: Eu tenho certeza de que vai dar certo.
english: I'm sure it's going to work out.
old: 'Ter certeza' means 'to be sure' – literally 'to have certainty.' 'Dar certo' means 'to work out' and is one of the most useful Brazilian expressions.
focus: One rule only: 'dar certo' is literally 'to give right' = to work out; drop the ter certeza half (pt-0343 already owns the ter-for-be pattern).

target: Ela é advogada, mas está trabalhando como professora.
english: She's a lawyer, but she's working as a teacher.
old: 'Ser' for profession (permanent identity) vs 'estar' for current activity (temporary). She IS a lawyer but she's currently working as a teacher.
focus: Insight is perfect for this card but quotes nothing from it: anchor with 'é advogada' (identity) vs 'está trabalhando' (what she's doing right now).

target: Quem ligou para você?
english: Who called you?
old: 'Quem ligou' = who called. 'Ligar para' = to call (someone). 'Para' is required with 'ligar.'
focus: The earn is 'ligar para': you call TO someone in Portuguese ('ligou para você'), no direct object like English – cut the who-called re-translation.

target: Estou animado para a viagem.
english: I'm looking forward to the trip.
old: por = reason / exchange / route. para = destination / purpose / recipient. trabalho por dinheiro (for money) vs trabalho para o futuro (for the future).
focus: Anchor por-vs-para in this card's 'para a viagem' (para = toward a goal/destination); cut the generic trabalho por/para job examples.

target: Ela trabalha na recepção do hotel.
english: She works at the hotel reception.
old: 'Na recepção' = em + a = at/in the. 'Recepção' is feminine – nouns ending in -ção are always feminine.
focus: One rule: nouns in -ção are always feminine ('a recepção'); cut the em + a contraction half (pt-0480 covers contractions).

target: O mapa da cidade está no celular.
english: The city map is on the phone.
old: 'Mapa' is masculine despite ending in -a: o mapa. Other exceptions: o dia, o cinema, o problema, o tema, o sistema.
focus: Keep 'o mapa' masculine-despite--a as the trap; trim the exception list to one or two siblings (the -ma pattern: o problema, o sistema)

target: A estação do metrô fica a dois quarteirões.
english: The subway station is two blocks away.
old: 'Ficar' for permanent locations: 'o hotel fica perto' = the hotel is (located) near. More specific than 'estar.'
focus: ficar = fixed location (vs estar) is the insight – use this card's own 'a estação fica a dois quarteirões' as the example, not the hotel sentence

target: Qual é o seu nome?
english: What's your name?
old: 'Qual' means 'which/what' when choosing from options or asking for specific information. 'Qual é o seu nome?' is the standard way to ask someone's name.
focus: The trap is that it's 'Qual é o seu nome?' not 'O que' – lead with that English-default mistake, cut the definition padding

target: O que você está lendo?
english: What are you reading?
old: `estar + gerúndio` = English '-ing right now': `estou comendo` = 'I'm eating'. Brazilians use this way more than Spanish/Italian use their gerundios.
focus: estar + gerund = right-now '-ing' (and Brazilians use it constantly) – strip the backticks and anchor with this card's 'está lendo', not 'estou comendo'
